intro: Delft's oldest tree predates the Netherlands' own royal house by two centuries and still fruits every summer in a working almshouse courtyard. Its youngest tree is a graft from Germany, planted specifically to keep William of Orange's memory rooted in the city where he died. Eight verified trees, one of them a living link to a 1944 discovery once thought extinct.
meta_description: Delft's oldest tree is a 319-year-old mulberry in a 1707 almshouse courtyard. Eight verified ancient trees, real stories, how to reach each one.
question_answer: Delft's oldest tree is a black mulberry in the courtyard of Hofje van Pauw on Paardenmarkt, planted in 1707 when the almshouse was founded and roughly 319 years old. Tree specialist Jorn Copijn identified it in 2023 as a rare subspecies likely brought to the Netherlands by the VOC.
question_meta: A 319-year-old mulberry in a 1707 almshouse courtyard is Delft's oldest tree. Where to find it, and the city's other seven verified ancient trees.
question_context: The mulberry's age comes from the founding date of Hofje van Pauw itself, the almshouse Elisabeth Pauw endowed by testament in 1707, rather than a ring count or measured estimate. Copijn Boomspecialisten's 2023 assessment identified the tree as Morus nigra subsp. multicaulus, a subspecies not formally recorded in Europe until 1821, well over a century after this specimen was already growing in the courtyard. The most likely explanation ties the tree to Delft's own trading history rather than European botany: the Dutch East India Company traded out of India, where the subspecies originates, from 1700, and kept a chamber in Delft from 1602, making a returning VOC ship a more plausible route for the tree than any documented import. The hofje's courtyard gate on Paardenmarkt stays open to visitors during the day, though the houses around the tree are still lived in. None of Delft's other verified trees currently outdate it; the next oldest, a set of horse chestnuts on Sint Agathaplein, is over two centuries younger.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Delft?
faq.a: A black mulberry in the courtyard of Hofje van Pauw on Paardenmarkt, planted in 1707 when the almshouse was founded, roughly 319 years old.

faq.q: Are Delft's ancient trees free to visit?
faq.a: The mulberry's courtyard and Sint Agathaplein are both free public access, as are the newly added Kalverbos elms and planes and the wingnut and bald cypress on the old Nieuwe Plantage rampart. The Prinsentuin linden sits on Museum Prinsenhof's grounds, which are mid-renovation through 2027, so garden access may be temporarily restricted. TU Delft's Botanic Garden, home to the dawn redwoods, charges standard admission.

faq.q: Why does Delft have a tree grown from a twig cut in Germany?
faq.a: The Prinsentuin's winter linden, planted in 1956, grew from a cutting of the Wilhelmslinde in Dillenburg, the tree William of Orange grew up beside before leading the Dutch revolt and being assassinated in Delft in 1584. Supporters planted its cuttings at sites tied to his life.

faq.q: What are the dawn redwoods at TU Delft's Botanic Garden?
faq.a: Two Metasequoia glyptostroboides, a species known only from fossils until a living stand was found in China in 1944. Delft's specimens descend from the 1947 international seed collection that followed, making them among the first of their species grown in Europe.

trees.name: The Black Mulberry of Hofje van Pauw
trees.story: The black mulberry in the courtyard of Hofje van Pauw has been fruiting since before the Dutch East India Company's Delft chamber was a century old. Tree specialist Jorn Copijn identified it in 2023 as Morus nigra subsp. multicaulus, a subspecies not officially recorded in Europe until 1821, more than a century after this specimen was already growing here. The likely explanation involves no botanist at all: the VOC had traded out of India, where the subspecies originates, since 1700, and Delft kept its own VOC chamber from 1602, so a sea captain or merchant returning home is the more probable route than any recorded introduction. At 319 years old it ranks among the oldest fruit trees documented in the Netherlands. The hofje itself, an almshouse Elisabeth Pauw endowed by testament in 1707 for women who had fallen on hard times, still houses residents today, now adults with intellectual disabilities, and the tree has outlived every one of them. Its courtyard gate on Paardenmarkt stays unlocked during the day. Visitors are asked to keep to the garden and skip the windows, since the houses ringing the tree are still lived in, not a museum.
trees.access: Free, public courtyard accessible via the gatehouse during the day; the surrounding houses are private residences, please respect residents' privacy
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 10-minute walk

best_time.label: July to August: dark fruit that stains everything under the tree

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by fruiting in the courtyard of an almshouse founded in 1707, its black mulberries among the oldest fruit trees documented in the Netherlands. It stands behind the unlocked gate of Hofje van Pauw on Paardenmarkt.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnuts of Sint Agathaplein
trees.species: Horse Chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum and Aesculus x carnea)
trees.story: Five horse chestnuts on Sint Agathaplein, three white-flowered and two red, have stood outside the building where William of Orange was shot dead since 1920, planted as part of a coordinated square-wide planting rather than growing in on their own. The address carries more history than the trees themselves: Museum Prinsenhof occupies the former convent where William, leader of the Dutch revolt against Spanish rule, was assassinated on the staircase in 1584, and the bullet holes are still in the wall inside. De Boominspecteurs, commissioned by the municipality to assess the square's trees ahead of a major renovation, confirmed the chestnuts as part of the site's protected planting. The renovation itself started in 2025 and is due to finish in 2027, with the museum closed for the duration, and the municipality has stated the square's monumental trees are being kept in the new design even where other, younger planting is not. What that means for a visitor right now is straightforward caution rather than a locked gate: Sint Agathaplein is a public square, but a live building site sits next to it, so the usual free, unrestricted access may be temporarily altered until the work finishes.
trees.access: Sint Agathaplein is a free public square; an active construction site next door (the Prinsenhof renovation, underway to 2027) may temporarily affect the immediate surroundings
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 10-minute walk
trees.notes: Planting year (1920) and species mix (3 white, 2 red) sourced from De Boominspecteurs' 2024/2025 municipal assessment; independently corroborated by the municipality's own 2007 monumental-trees register, which lists the same square, count and species split (though without a planting date). Flagged for the ongoing Prinsenhof renovation (started 2025, due 2027): the municipality has stated its monumental trees are being kept in the new design, but current day-to-day access to the immediate area may vary while construction continues.
trees.how_to_recognise: You are looking for five chestnuts rather than one tree, three of them white-flowered and two red. They stand on Sint Agathaplein outside the Prinsenhof, with the building site next door.

trees.name: The Willemslinde of the Prinsentuin

location.address: Prinsentuin, Museum Prinsenhof, Sint Agathaplein 1, Delft

trees.story: This winter linden did not grow from a seed that fell nearby. It grew from a twig cut from the Wilhelmslinde in Dillenburg, Germany, the tree under which William of Orange spent his childhood before he became the reluctant leader of the Dutch revolt and was assassinated in Delft in 1584. Supporters of the House of Orange took cuttings from the Dillenburg original and planted them at sites tied to William's life, and this one went into the Prinsentuin, the garden beside Museum Prinsenhof, in 1956. It is by a wide margin the youngest tree on this list, not even a century old against the mulberry's three, but it carries the most direct physical link to the man Delft is built around commemorating. The museum grounds are mid-renovation as of 2026, work that started in 2025 and runs to 2027, and the municipality has said the garden's historic trees are being kept rather than cleared for the new design. Until the museum reopens, treat the Prinsentuin as a garden worth checking on rather than one guaranteed open on any given day.
trees.access: Museum Prinsenhof and its garden are mid-renovation (started 2025, due to reopen 2027-2028); the municipality has confirmed the garden's historic trees are being kept, but the Prinsentuin itself may not be openly walkable until the work finishes, check current status before visiting
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 10-minute walk
trees.notes: The 1956 planting date and Dillenburg-graft story come from De Boominspecteurs' municipal assessment; the Dillenburg connection is independently corroborated by the Wilhelmslinde's own official Dillenburg tourism page, which confirms cuttings from the original tree were planted at sites tied to William of Orange's life, though it does not itself name Delft's exact planting year. Flagged mainly for the live construction context: the garden is inside an active renovation site as of 2026, so treat the access note above as load-bearing, not a formality.

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by how young it is, a lime planted in 1956 from a cutting off the Dillenburg original. It stands in the Prinsentuin, the garden beside Museum Prinsenhof.

trees.name: The Dawn Redwoods of TU Delft's Botanic Garden
trees.age_estimate: age undocumented, among the first of the species grown in Europe after its 1944 rediscovery

location.address: Botanic Garden TU Delft, Poortlandplein 6, Delft

trees.story: Every dawn redwood alive today, anywhere in the world, descends from a single discovery: a species known only from 150-million-year-old fossils, presumed extinct, until a forester found a living stand of it in a remote Chinese valley in 1944. An international seed-collecting expedition followed in 1947, and botanical gardens across Europe, including several in the Netherlands, raised their first Metasequoia glyptostroboides from that single haul. Two of them now dominate the middle section of TU Delft's Botanic Garden, tall enough to be the garden's own reference point long before a visitor reaches the rarer specimens around them. Nobody recorded the exact planting year for these two, so no source gives a precise age, only the certainty that they belong to the first generation of the species ever grown outside China since its rediscovery, making them roughly seventy to eighty years old by extension rather than by record. The garden charges standard admission and sits a short walk from Delft's main station, a working research collection rather than a park, with the redwoods' feathery, deciduous foliage turning copper in autumn before it drops, unusual for a conifer and part of what first convinced botanists this was something genuinely new.
trees.access: Paid entry, standard botanic garden admission
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 15-minute walk, or tram/bus to TU Noord
trees.notes: Both sources (TU Delft's own garden guide and the Dutch Dendrological Society) independently describe these two Metasequoia as among the earliest planted in the Netherlands following the species' 1944 rediscovery and the 1947 international seed-collecting expedition, but neither gives an exact planting year for the Delft specimens specifically. No age is asserted (age_min/max left at 0) rather than guessed; the roughly 70-80 year figure implied by the story text is explicitly framed as inference from the species' introduction history, not a documented date. No qualifying photo found (Commons category for TU Delft's garden has no Metasequoia-specific image); genuine gap.
trees.how_to_recognise: You are looking for two of them rather than one tree, standing together and dominating the middle section of the garden, taller than anything you pass on the way in.

trees.name: The Planes of Kalverbos
trees.story:
Three plane trees went into Kalverbos around the years Delft finished the red-brick water tower that still looms over the park. Construction started in 1895, the tower pumped the city's water until 1996 and has since become a venue for parties. The register that protects these trees describes them standing in the same historic setting as the tower, an old bench and the graves nearby, planted as the park found its final shape.

Kalverbos itself began as a cemetery, in use for 46 years before Delft moved its dead to the Jaffalaan in 1874. Its conversion into a public park in 1894, laid out by garden architect Hugo Poortman in the romantic landscape style, gave it the winding paths it still has. These planes, dated to 1890 to 1900, are close to that age, among the first trees to grow up with the park rather than the burial ground it replaced.

London planes are a seventeenth century hybrid of an American and an Asian parent, fast growing and tolerant enough of clipping to survive on a Dutch street. Three of them, standing together at well over a century old, anchor one corner of a park that covers barely a hectare.
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen v2024 (Bomenstichting), register nr 1697031: Platanen Kalverbos, three trees, Kalverbos, Delft, planting band 1890-1900, reason for protection 'monumentaal', owner gemeente, recorded as visitable and visible
trees.access: Free, in the open park of Kalverbos, at any hour
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 15-minute walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as three plane trees standing together well over a century old. They stand near Kalverbos's red-brick water tower and the park's remaining graves.

trees.name: The Wingnut of Nieuwe Plantage
trees.story:
A wingnut gets its name from a seed built with two papery blades, and this one has grown for well over a century on ground that used to be Delft's city wall. The wall came down around 1890, and the register credits the new layout to a landscape architect surnamed Zocher, a name attached to some of the country's best known nineteenth century parks, who chose large, fast-growing species for the reclaimed rampart. That is the register's own account of why this edge of the city carries so many good trees planted at once.

Caucasian wingnuts come from forests around the Black Sea and the Caspian, and they grow faster than almost anything else planted alongside them in a Dutch garden, oaks and limes included. This one was planted between 1890 and 1900, putting it at around 130 years old, on a strip of the old rampart directly across the street from an ordinary Delft address, number 28 Nieuwe Plantage.

Nothing beyond the national monumental tree register has been found to confirm it further. If you know this tree, tell us.
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen v2024 (Bomenstichting), register nr 1696370: Vleugelnoot, Tegenover Nieuwe Plantage 28, Delft, planting band 1890-1900, reason for protection 'monumentaal', owner gemeente, recorded as visitable and visible
trees.access: Free, on the public verge opposite Nieuwe Plantage 28, at any hour
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 15-minute walk

best_time.label: July to September: long green catkins of winged nutlets hang from every branch

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the two papery-bladed seeds of a wingnut and fast, wide growth. It stands on the old city rampart opposite Nieuwe Plantage 28.

trees.name: The Bald Cypress of Geer Boogerd
trees.story:
A swamp tree from the American South outlived the psychiatric hospital that once surrounded it. The Sint-Jorisgasthuis stood on this ground for close to 150 years under its older name, Binnengesticht, rebuilt in the 1920s and finally demolished in the 1960s to make way for housing. Its bald cypress, planted somewhere between 1910 and 1920 in what was then the institution's large garden, is one of the few things on the site that survived the building coming down around it.

Bald cypresses are conifers that behave like broadleaf trees, dropping their needles every autumn, which is unusual enough among cone-bearing species that Delft's specimen stands out on a small square that gives no other hint of what stood here for a century and a half. In its native range along the Mississippi and the Gulf coast it grows in standing water and throws up woody knees around its base; on a Dutch street corner it just grows tall.

At around 110 years old, it is the youngest of Delft's newly registered trees and the only witness left to a building nobody living remembers walking into.

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn rust orange before dropping

verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen v2024 (Bomenstichting), register nr 1696368: Moerascypres, Geer Boogerd 57-59, Delft, planting band 1910-1920, reason for protection 'monumentaal', owner gemeente, recorded as visitable and visible
trees.access: Free, on the public square at Geer Boogerd, at any hour
trees.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 15-minute walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a conifer that drops its needles every autumn like a broadleaf tree, unusual among cone-bearers. It stands alone on the small square at Geer Boogerd.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of the Botterbrug

location.address: Next to the former girls' orphanage, Oude Delft 116 at the Botterbrug, Delft

trees.access: Free. Municipal garden at the Oude Delft canal and Botterbrug, listed visitable and visible in the register.
trees.transport: About 0.5 km north of Delft station; a few minutes' walk from the Markt via Oude Delft.
trees.story:
Nothing else on this stretch of the Oude Delft comes close: seen from above, the plane tree at the Botterbrug is one broad round crown spreading over the canal edge, the largest along the water here. It stands in a small municipal garden beside the former girls' orphanage at Oude Delft 116, and the national register of monumental trees lists it as open to visit and visible from the street.

That register is also where its age comes from. It puts the planting somewhere between 1880 and 1890, which makes the tree about 140 years old, give or take a decade. It records nothing else: no story behind the planting, no name of whoever chose the spot, and no measurement of the trunk.

What the tree has lived through is easier to say. It was already well grown when Delft was occupied in 1940, and it has watched well over a century of boats on the canal and walkers crossing the bridge. Like every London plane it sheds its bark in plates, so the trunk is a patchwork of grey, olive and cream.

The register counts it as a single tree standing on its own rather than one of a row. Nobody has published its girth or its height. If you have put a tape measure round it, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its crown, the single largest along this stretch of the Oude Delft. It stands at the Botterbrug bridge, beside the former girls' orphanage at Oude Delft 116.

trees.name: The Plane Tree at the Annageer corner

location.address: Nieuwe Plantage at the corner with Annageer, Delft

trees.access: Free. Public park strip on the old rampart (Nieuwe Plantage), listed visitable in the register.
trees.transport: About 1.2 km north-west of Delft station; the Plantage ring is a 15 minute walk from the Markt.
trees.story:
The whole recorded history of this plane tree is one line in the national register: it was planted during the renovation of Delft's city ramparts. The line gives no year. What the register does give is a planting band of 1880 to 1890, which puts the tree at roughly 130 to 145 years old, and that band is the only date anybody has published for it.

It stands where the Nieuwe Plantage meets the Annageer, on the strip of park that now runs along the old rampart line. From above it is one large rounded crown at the junction of the paths, touching its neighbours but plainly its own tree. The register files it under the municipality, in a park setting, open to visit.

In its time on the old wall the tree has stood through the occupation of 1940 to 1945 and well over a century of Delft walking past on its way somewhere else. Like every London plane it sheds its bark in plates, leaving the trunk a patchwork of grey, olive and cream.

It is also the start of a short walk. The elms of Kalverbos stand about 90 metres away, with that park's three planes close beside them. Nobody has published this tree's girth or height; if you have measured it, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the large rounded crown right at the path junction where the Nieuwe Plantage meets the Annageer. It stands about 90 metres from the Kalverbos elms; its crown touches its neighbours'.

trees.name: The Ash of the Oostpoort
trees.access: Free. Public lawn beside the canal at the Oostpoort gate (plantsoen), listed visitable and visible in the register.
trees.transport: About 1 km east of Delft station, roughly 0.8 km east of the Markt along the canal; the Oostpoort is signposted as a sight.
trees.verify_notes: Writing pass 2026-10-08: findable only by the species tell. The register pin falls between two crowns on the lawn (~6 m SW, ~10 m N) and no source says which is the ash or what the other tree is, so the recognition line leans on ash leaves and buds, which settles it only if the neighbour is not also an ash. Not made fully findable: needs a photograph of the trunk or a reader report naming which crown. Story asks the reader. Kept location_precision approximate with location_site as verified.
trees.story:
The gate is the famous one, but the ash on the lawn beside it is no medieval relic: the national register of monumental trees puts its planting between 1880 and 1890, centuries after the gate itself was built. That band makes the tree about 140 years old, give or take a decade, and it is the only date anybody has published for it.

It stands on a small municipal lawn by the canal at the Oostpoort quay, a plantsoen in the register's own word, listed as open to visit and visible from the path. The register records it as a single tree and says nothing about who planted it or why.

Surviving this long as an ash is its own small achievement. Ash dieback, a fungus that reached Europe in the 1990s, has been killing ashes across the continent, the Netherlands included. The most recent aerial photograph shows the crowns on this lawn still in leaf.

One honest caveat. The register's pin falls between two trees on the lawn, one a few metres south-west and one a little further north, and nobody has yet said which of them is the ash. If you stand there, the leaves settle it: an ash carries its leaflets in opposite pairs along a single stalk. Tell us which one it is, and send a photograph if you take one.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves, small leaflets in opposite pairs along one stalk, and black buds in winter. It stands on the small lawn by the canal at the Oostpoort, one of two trees the pin falls between.
